title: Here am I, send me (Isaiah 6)
hook: Isaiah sees the Lord, the seraphs cry holy, and a coal touches his lips

segments.voice: Yesterday, the exile: Jerusalem burned, and the people wept by the waters of Babylon. Your line was by the waters again. Who far from home did you remember? Day four hundred fifteen.

Every Sunday at Mass, just before the Eucharistic Prayer, the whole church sings or says the Sanctus, the song that calls God holy three times over and says heaven and earth are full of his glory. Today we find where it comes from. We step back in time now, before the exile, to the prophets who warned it was coming. One of them is Isaiah, Isaias in the Douay-Rheims. And his book turns on a single moment in the Temple, in the year King Uzziah died, Ozias in the Douay, when a man looks up and sees more than he ever wanted to see.
screen: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY AT EVERY MASS.` → `BACK BEFORE THE EXILE.` → `THE YEAR KING UZZIAH DIED.`

segments.voice: In the Douay: "I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and elevated: and his train filled the temple." Just the hem of God's robe fills the whole building. Above him stand seraphim, a name usually taken to mean burning ones, each with six wings: two to cover the face, two to cover the feet, two to fly. And they call to each other: "Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory." The doorposts shake. Smoke fills the house. And Isaiah's first reaction isn't wonder. It's terror. "Woe is me," he says, because I am a man of unclean lips, living among a people of unclean lips, and my eyes have seen the King. He's undone. Then one of the seraphim flies to him holding a live coal, taken with tongs from the altar, and touches his mouth with it: thy iniquities shall be taken away, and thy sin shall be cleansed. Not punishment. Cleansing. And only then does God speak, not to Isaiah but almost to himself: "Whom shall I send? and who shall go for us?" And the man who a moment ago said woe is me answers: "Lo, here am I, send me." In Hebrew, here am I is a single word, hineni. Abraham says it. Moses says it at the bush. The boy Samuel says it in the night. It means I'm present, I'm listening, use me. Catholics have kept this scene close. The seraphim's cry became the Sanctus at every Mass. And in the older form of the Mass, the priest prays before reading the Gospel that God would cleanse his lips as he cleansed the lips of Isaiah with a burning coal.
screen: `HIS TRAIN FILLED THE TEMPLE.` · `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.` · `WOE IS ME: UNCLEAN LIPS.` · `A COAL FROM THE ALTAR.` · then, large: `LO, HERE AM I, SEND ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say send me about one task. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing that needs doing that nobody has volunteered for. At home, at work, in your parish or neighborhood. The dishes nobody claims. The hard phone call. The meal for the family that just had a baby. If something in you says woe is me, I'm not the right person, Isaiah said that too. Then, quietly, say his words about that one task: here am I, send me. If you pray, say them to God. The bell holds the time.
Here am I. In Hebrew, hineni: present, listening, ready. Isaiah's answer after the coal touched his lips: here am I, send me. Today's word.
Your line: here am I, send me. Today, volunteer for the one task you named, before anyone has to ask twice. Day four hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: At every Mass, Catholics sing or say the Sanctus, Holy, holy, holy, drawn from the seraphim's cry in Isaiah 6, and the call of Isaiah is often read at ordinations and on Sundays about vocation.

fork.setup: you're Isaiah. you've seen the Lord, your lips have just been touched with a burning coal, and you hear: whom shall I send? what do you say?
options: nothing; it wasn't said to you.
fork.reveal: Isaiah answers: lo, here am I, send me. the same man who said woe is me a moment before.

original.note: Hebrew: here I am, one word. Said by Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Isaiah when God calls.

trapdoor: what you thought: a brave prophet signs up for a mission.
what it means: a terrified man sees God's holiness, is cleansed by a coal from the altar, and only then says send me.
what a scholar hears: hineni, the answer of Abraham, Moses and Samuel. and the seraphim's song became the Sanctus of the Mass.

sources.ref: Roman Missal of 1962, the prayer Munda cor meum

notes: Uzziah's death dated around 740 BC (estimates c. 742–736); confirm 'around 740'.

The Munda cor meum prayer before the Gospel in the 1962 Missal refers to cleansing Isaiah's lips with a burning coal; paraphrased. A version is also in the current Missal ('Cleanse my heart and my lips'); confirm whether to say 'still today'.
Seraphim as 'burning ones' (from saraph): standard; confirm.
The hard commission in 6:9–13 is omitted.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'most Catholics could say it in their sleep', 'the first and longest' prophet, 'around 740 BC', 'a young man' and 'for centuries' (claims rule); seraphim etymology softened; added the quoted 'Woe is me' (6:5) and the hineni passages to sources; practice no longer tells the listener what they feel.
